Harriet Tubman. An enslaved woman who escaped bondage and became the most famous conductor of the Underground Railroad, risking her life repeatedly to guide approximately seventy enslaved people to freedom in the North. Born in Maryland's Eastern Shore, she endured severe brutality but escaped in eighteen-forty-nine, then returned to the South at least thirteen times to lead others to liberty. During the American Civil War, she served the Union Army as a nurse, cook, and scout, becoming a legendary symbol of Black resistance and self-determination.

Harriet suffered brutal treatment under multiple enslavers, including whippings so severe they left permanent scars and neurological damage. She escaped to Philadelphia in eighteen-forty-nine after attempting escape years earlier and being recaptured and sold farther south. Once free, she earned the nickname Moses for leading enslaved people out of bondage, comparing herself to the Biblical figure who freed the Hebrews.

She had an extraordinarily high success rate. All of her passengers reached freedom safely, a remarkable feat that earned her deep trust and legendary status. She used the North Star and hidden safe houses, called stations, of the Underground Railroad network to navigate hundreds of miles to Pennsylvania, New York, and Canada.

During the Civil War, she served at Fort Wagner as a nurse and cook, and participated in the Combahee River Raid in eighteen-sixty-three, which liberated over seven hundred enslaved people. She lived until nineteen-thirteen, continuing activism for women's suffrage and African American education in her later years.
